passages.title: Passage 1
passages.instructions:
Questions 1–40

You should spend about 60 minutes on Questions 1–40, which are based on the reading passage below.
passages.body:
Bilingual Education Policy

A Bilingual education policy debates how schools should teach students fluent in a home language different from the dominant language of instruction, balancing rapid acquisition of societal lingua franca with maintenance of heritage languages linked to identity, cognition, and family communication. Models include transitional programmes fading home language support after a few years, dual-language immersion enrolling both majority and minority speakers, and English-only mandates historically associated with assimilationist goals now contested by research documenting benefits of sustained bilingualism for executive function and literacy transfer when pedagogy is high quality not simply sink-or-swim submersion blamed for dropout disparities among linguistic minorities tracked into low expectations remedial tracks devoid of grade-level content—a civil

B Canada's French immersion programmes produced generations of anglophone bilinguals, informing exportable models though context differs where minority language enjoys constitutional protection unlike immigrant tongues. US Lau remedies required districts to address language barriers after landmark litigation, spawning ESL pull-out sessions sometimes fragmenting instructional time insufficiently integrating content and language objectives co-taught by subject and language specialists collaboratively a best practice still rare due to staffing shortages and professional development gaps leaving paraprofessionals supervising drills disconnected from science and history curricula students need for graduation requirements closing college pathways systematically. New Zealand recognises Māori medium schools reviving te reo, coupling language revitalisation with indigenous sovereignty politics, demonstrating education policy inseparable from

C Cognitive research indicates balanced bilinguals may develop enhanced metalinguistic awareness and task-switching abilities, though effects depend on proficiency levels and socioeconomic supports at home—libraries, tutoring—not language status alone. Critics citing test score gaps sometimes ignore that newcomers arrive mid-year facing trauma from migration; with appropriate sheltered instruction, gaps narrow over time in well-resourced districts while under-resourced counterparts blame bilingual programmes scapegoating them for funding inequities truly causing failure. Standardised assessments in only dominant language underestimate content knowledge demonstrable in home language portfolios reviewers could evaluate bilingually if policy allowed, biasing accountability systems punishing schools serving immigrants courageously while affluent districts with few English learners appear high performing on narrow metrics

D Teacher preparation programmes increasingly require ESL endorsements and sociolinguistic coursework, yet veteran teachers resist retrofitting practices without paid planning time. Credential reciprocity across states and countries lags, wasting skilled immigrant teachers driving taxis despite shortage of bilingual educators—a labour market failure policy could fix with accelerated certification and fair pay scales recognising specialisation instead of exploitative stipends temporary fellows receive then burn out. Curriculum materials culturally responsive and linguistically graded remain scarce commercial publishers underinvest low-incidence language pairs, pushing districts to develop open educational resources collaboratively online sharing lesson plans adapting universal design principles benefiting all learners including monolingual English speakers exposed to global perspectives widening parochial curricula historically centring

E Assessment policy for reclassifying students as fluent affects funding formulas incentivising premature exit from language services before academic readiness, a gaming risk auditors flag recommending multiple criteria including classroom performance and parent consultation not single test cutoffs high-stakes for school ratings corrupting incentives. Summer programmes and after-school heritage classes supplement school day, involving families as partners literate in home languages asked to volunteer reading stories reinforcing biliteracy joy not drill killing motivation among children proud yet anxious performing identity in playgrounds policing accents cruelly peer-driven unless schools cultivate inclusive climates explicitly anti-bullying with restorative practices addressing linguistic harassment intersecting racism frequently reported in ethnographic studies guidance counsellors undertrained to handle,

F Political cycles swing policy: bilingual bans in some US states later softened; Europe debates integration contracts requiring language exams for residency, conflating civic belonging with monolingual ideals contested by multilingual cities where half of pupils speak another home language normatively. Digital translators and AI tutors may assist practice but cannot replace human interaction developing pragmatic competence and socioemotional confidence participating in debates, lab experiments, and literature circles requiring nuanced expression machines approximate awkwardly still though improving rapidly posing future policy choices about resource allocation supplementing not supplanting teachers central to relationship-rich education adolescents especially need during identity formation volatile years when language shame silences participation harming learning broadly across subjects

G Looking ahead, the author advocates evidence-based bilingual models with adequate funding, teacher pipelines, and fair accountability. Heritage language maintenance supports family cohesion and global skills simultaneously. Policies should resist scapegoating multilingualism for inequality caused by austerity and segregation. Pilots expanding dual immersion in diverse districts build political coalitions when parents see benefits for all children. If education systems treat bilingualism as problem not resource, societies waste human capital and repeat historical assimilation harms now discredited ethically and empirically. Inclusive policy frames linguistic diversity as public good deserving constitutional protection and budget lines matching rhetoric celebrating diversity on websites with real materials, staffing, and assessment justice delivering equitable pathways to universities
